## 🏠 Minimum Barrier Height – Deck on a House

### When is a barrier required?
Under **NZBC Clause F4.3.1**, a barrier is required wherever people could **fall 1 metre or more** from an opening, floor edge, or sudden change in level associated with a building (such as a deck).

### Minimum Height
Under **F4/AS1 (Acceptable Solution), Table 1**, the minimum barrier height for a **house deck** is:

> **1,000 mm** (1 metre) measured from the deck surface to the top of the barrier.

### Additional Requirements for Housing
Because houses are **always considered likely to be frequented by children under 6**, the barrier must also:
- Have **no openings that a 100 mm diameter sphere can pass through** — across the full height of the barrier
- Be **continuous** and extend the full extent of the hazard
- Be **rigid and strong** enough to withstand the foreseeable impact and pressure of people

### Balustrade / Balcony Note
The same 1,000 mm minimum applies to balconies and similar deck-level areas in housing under F4/AS1.

---

### Key Practical Reminders:
| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Barrier trigger | Fall of **≥ 1 m** |
| Minimum height | **1,000 mm** |
| Max sphere through openings | **100 mm** |
| Stair triangular opening | **150 mm** sphere |

---

**Source: F4 Safety From Falling (third edition, unamended) · F4/AS1 · page 13 of 22; NZ Building Code Handbook 3rd Ed (amendment 13) · page 56 of 226**

## 🏊 Residential Pool Fence (Barrier) Height — NZ Building Code Clause F9

Pool fencing for residential pools is governed by **Building Code Clause F9 – Means of Restricting Access to Residential Pools**, with the detailed requirements set out in the Acceptable Solution **F9/AS1**.

### Why it exists
The purpose is to **prevent unsupervised access by children under 5 years of age** to any residential pool with 400 mm or more of water depth.

---

### 📏 Minimum Heights (F9/AS1)

| Location of Barrier | Minimum Height |
|---|---|
| **Not on a property boundary** (freestanding pool fence) | **1,200 mm** above finished ground/floor level on the outside |
| **Wire mesh with openings 13–35 mm** (a specific material type) | **1,800 mm** minimum |

> ⚠️ Note: Section 2.2 of F9/AS1 covers pool barriers **on a property boundary** — the retrieved pages indicate specific rules apply in that case too. You should review this section carefully in the full document, as boundary fences used as pool barriers have additional requirements.

---

### 📋 Other Key Requirements (F9/AS1)

- The barrier **must not be angled more than 15° from vertical**, and may only slope *away* from the pool
- **No openings** through which a **100 mm diameter sphere** could pass
- Non-vertical rails/wires must be **at least 900 mm apart vertically** to restrict climbing
- **No objects or ground features** within **1,200 mm of the top** of the barrier on the outside that could assist climbing
- Projections on the outside face must not have a horizontal projection **greater than 10 mm** (unless at least 900 mm apart vertically)

### 🚪 Gates must:
- Open **away from the pool**
- **Not be readily opened by children**
- **Automatically return** to the closed position after use

### 📄 Building Consent Required
Pool barriers always require a **building consent** — they are explicitly excluded from the general fence consent exemption.

---

**Source: F9 Restricting Access to Residential Pools · F9 Restricting Access to Residential Pools · page 11 of 19**

## Maximum Hot Water Temperature at a Bath or Shower (Residential)

Under **Acceptable Solution G12/AS1, Paragraph 6.14.1**, the maximum delivered hot water temperature at any sanitary fixture used for personal hygiene (including **baths, showers, hand basins, and bidets**) is:

| Building Type | Maximum Temperature |
|---|---|
| **Houses and all other buildings** (not in the list below) | **50°C** |
| Early childhood centres, schools, old people's homes, institutions for people with psychiatric/physical disabilities, hospitals | **45°C** |

> ⚠️ **Note:** The Ministry of Education also requires that taps accessible to children in **early childhood education and care centres** do not exceed **40°C** for licensing purposes.

### How is this achieved?
A **tempering valve (TV)** or **thermostatic mixing valve (TMV)** is required to control the delivered temperature. The water heater itself may store water at a higher temperature (for legionella control), but the mixed/tempered water delivered to the fixture must not exceed the limits above.

---

*This is general NZ Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice. Please confirm against the current official G12/AS1 document and consult your designer or licensed plumber for anything safety-critical.*

## Ground Clearance — Bottom of Wall Cladding to Unpaved Ground

### Concrete Slab Floor (most common)
Per **E2/AS1 clause 9.1.2.6**, the base of the cladding system must finish a minimum of:

| Surface type | Minimum clearance |
|---|---|
| **Unpaved (bare/landscaped ground)** | **175 mm** |
| Paved surface | 100 mm |

In addition, the cladding must:
- **Overlap the concrete slab by at least 50 mm**
- Be **offset horizontally by a minimum of 6 mm** (for direct-fixed claddings) to prevent capillary action

### Timber Floor Framing
Per **E2/AS1 clause 9.1.2.8 & Table 9.1.2.1**, clearances from unpaved surfaces to wall framing are in accordance with **NZS 3604**, and the base of the cladding must overlap the timber floor structure by **50 mm minimum**.

---

### ⚠️ A few important points:
- **NZS 3604 may require greater clearances** depending on floor type and materials — always check both documents.
- **Final landscaped ground levels** must be taken into account during design — don't let earthworks or landscaping later eat into your clearance.
- Reduced clearances (e.g. under a sheltered overhang above well-drained paving) would need to be designed and consented as an **alternative solution**.

---

### 🏗️ Minimum Cladding Clearance Above Paved Surfaces

For **concrete ground slabs** (excluding masonry veneer), the base of the cladding system must finish a minimum of:

| Surface Type | Minimum Clearance |
|---|---|
| **Paved surface** | **100 mm** |
| Unpaved/bare ground | 175 mm |
| Roof cladding or membrane deck | 35 mm |

> **E2/AS1, clause 9.1.2.6(a):** *"finish a minimum of (i) 100 mm above a paved surface, or (ii) 175 mm above finished unpaved surface."*

The cladding must also:
- **Overlap** the concrete slab by **50 mm minimum**
- Be **offset horizontally by at least 6 mm** (for direct-fixed claddings) to prevent capillary action

Clearances below these minimums *may* be considered (e.g., well-drained paving under a roof overhang), but these would need to be **designed and assessed as an alternative solution** — they can't simply be assumed.

### 🪜 Private Stairway Step Limits (NZ Building Code – D1/AS1, Table 6)

| Stair Type | Max Pitch | **Max Riser Height** | **Min Tread (Going)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Main private stairway** *(access to living areas, kitchens, garages & all exterior stairs)* | 37° | **190 mm** | **280 mm** |

- **Open risers** in areas frequented by children under 6 must not permit passage of a 100 mm sphere between treads.

## 🔶 Maximum Gradient for an Accessible Ramp

| Ramp Type | Maximum Slope |
|---|---|
| **Accessible ramp** | **1 in 12** |
| Common ramp (subject to wetting) | 1 in 10 |
| Common ramp (normally dry) | 1 in 8 |
| Service ramps | 1 in 3 |

So the steepest gradient permitted for an **accessible ramp** is **1:12**.

### Other key requirements for accessible ramps (D1/AS1):
- **Minimum clear width:** 1,200 mm
- **Upstand (kerb):** At least **75 mm** high on any drop-off side
- **Handrails:** Required on **both sides** where the ramp slope is steeper than **1 in 20**, and must be continuous (with a 300 mm horizontal extension at each end)
- **Cross fall:** No steeper than **1 in 50**
- **Landings** are required between ramp flights (maximum rise between landings applies — see Table 5 of D1/AS1)

---

---

## 🏗️ Structural Framing Durability — **50 Years Minimum**

Under **Building Code Clause B2 (Durability)** and its Acceptable Solution **B2/AS1**, structural framing must last **not less than 50 years**.

The decision framework in B2/AS1 (Figure 2.1.1.2) makes this clear:

> **Step 2:** *"If the building element provides structural stability to the building, then the durability requirement is 50 years."*

This applies directly to structural framing (wall framing, roof framing, floor framing, etc.), since it provides structural stability to the building.

---

### Key related elements also requiring ≥ 50 years:
| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Structural framing** | ✅ ≥ 50 years |
| **Bracing elements** (all situations) | ✅ ≥ 50 years |
| **Sub-floor structure** | ✅ ≥ 50 years |
| **DPC under structural framing members** | ✅ ≥ 50 years |
| **Fixings for structural elements** | ✅ ≥ 50 years |
| **Structural cladding (wall/roof)** | ✅ ≥ 50 years |

---

### How is this achieved in practice?
For **timber framing**, compliance is typically achieved by using:
- Treated timber meeting the requirements of **NZS 3602** and **NZS 3640** (referenced via NZS 3604), or
- The **Building Product Specifications (Subsection 3.5.1)** for 50-year durability

For **light steel framing**, **Clause 3 of the NASH Standard Part 2** can be used, provided the framing is within a closed building envelope performing to at least **E2/AS1** standard, with lined eaves.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm requirements against the current official MBIE documents and with your designer or engineer, especially for anything safety-critical.

Great news — the NZ Building Code is clear on this. Here's what G4/AS1 (the Acceptable Solution for Ventilation) requires for a bedroom (a habitable space):

---

## 🪟 Natural Ventilation — Bedroom Requirement

### The Core Rule
> **Net openable area of windows or other openings to the outside must be no less than 5% of the floor area of the room.**

So the calculation is simple:

| Bedroom Floor Area | Minimum Net Openable Window Area |
|---|---|
| 10 m² | 0.50 m² |
| 12 m² | 0.60 m² |
| 15 m² | 0.75 m² |
| 20 m² | 1.00 m² |

---

### ⚠️ Important Notes

1. **"Net openable area"** is the actual openable portion of the window — not the full glazed area. Fixed panes don't count.
2. **Single external wall (e.g. apartments):** If the bedroom has only one external wall and the room depth is less than 6 m, the same 5% rule applies to the openable windows on that wall, plus trickle ventilators are required (min. 2,000 mm² equivalent aerodynamic area each).
3. **Mechanical extract fans** (25 L/s) are separately required where there are showers or baths — natural ventilation alone is not sufficient for moisture removal in those spaces.
4. **Trickle ventilators** must be installed in all household unit habitable spaces (unless there is mechanical supply ventilation).

---

> ⚠️ *This is general NZ Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice. Always confirm against the current official G4/AS1 document on the MBIE website and check with your designer or consent authority for your specific project.*

## 🔊 NZ Building Code – Sound Insulation Between Apartments (Clause G6)

**Clause G6 – Airborne and Impact Sound** sets the minimum performance requirements for building elements (walls, floors, ceilings) **common between separate occupancies**, such as between two apartments.

### Minimum Ratings Required:

| Element | Metric | Minimum Rating |
|---|---|---|
| **Walls, Floors & Ceilings** (airborne sound) | **Sound Transmission Class (STC)** | **≥ 55** |
| **Floors** (impact sound) | **Impact Insulation Class (IIC)** | **≥ 55** |

### Key Code Clauses:
- **G6.1 (Objective):** Safeguard people from illness or loss of amenity due to undue noise transmitted between abutting occupancies.
- **G6.2 (Functional Requirement):** Building elements common between occupancies shall be constructed to prevent undue noise transmission to habitable spaces of household units.
- **G6.3.1:** STC of walls, floors, and ceilings shall be **no less than 55**.
- **G6.3.2:** IIC of floors shall be **no less than 55**.

### How is compliance demonstrated?
Compliance can be shown via **G6/VM1** (Verification Method), which references test standards such as **ASTM E 336** (airborne sound) and **ASTM E 492** (impact sound).

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm the current requirements against the official MBIE documents and with your designer or acoustic consultant — especially for safety-critical elements.

---

## 🔥 Smoke Alarms in a Residential House (NZ Building Code)

### The System Required
For a standard house (Risk Group **SH** – Single Household), the Building Code requires a **Type 1 – Domestic Smoke Alarm System**. This means:
- One or more **interconnected smoke alarm devices**, each with a smoke detector and audible alarm
- The system must comply with **NZS 4514** ("Interconnected smoke alarms for houses")

### Where Do They Go?
The specific room-by-room placement rules are set out in **NZS 4514**, which the Building Code references as the required standard. NZS 4514 generally requires alarms:

| Location | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Every bedroom** | ✅ Required |
| **Hallways** serving bedrooms | ✅ Required |
| **Living areas / lounge** | ✅ Required |
| **Each level/storey** of the house | ✅ At minimum one per level |
| **Kitchens** | ⚠️ Not typically a primary location — ionisation alarms should be kept away from cooking areas to avoid nuisance alarms |
| **Garages / roof spaces** | ❌ Not required |

### Key Installation Rules (from NZS 4514)
- All alarms must be **interconnected** (when one sounds, they all sound)
- Alarms must be mounted on **ceilings** where possible
- Must be kept **away from corners**, air vents, and cooking appliances
- Can be **battery-powered** (long-life 10-year) or **hardwired**

---

> ⚠️ **Important:** The detailed positioning rules (minimum distances from walls, vents, etc.) live inside **NZS 4514**, which is a purchased standard. Always confirm exact placement with your designer or the consent documents for this project, and check the current official documents at [building.govt.nz](https://www.building.govt.nz) for any amendments.

---

## NZ Building Code Clause E1 — Surface Water Design Storm Events

There are **two separate performance requirements** under NZBC Clause E1 for a residential house:

### 1. 📦 Disposal of Collected/Concentrated Surface Water — **10% AEP (1-in-10 year event)**
> *"Surface water resulting from an event having a **10% probability of occurring annually** and which is collected or concentrated by buildings or sitework, shall be disposed of in a way that avoids the likelihood of damage or nuisance to other property."*
> (E1.3.1)

- This applies to your **drainage systems** — gutters, downpipes, site drains, etc.
- The system must handle a 1-in-10 year storm without causing damage or nuisance to neighbouring properties.

---

### 2. 🏠 Preventing Water Entry into the Building — **2% AEP (1-in-50 year event)**
> *"Surface water resulting from an event having a **2% probability of occurring annually**, shall not enter buildings."*
> (E1.3.2)

- This applies to **floor level and site grading** — your floor must sit high enough that a 1-in-50 year event can't get inside.
- This requirement applies specifically to **Housing, Communal Residential, and Communal Non-residential** buildings.

---

### In Plain Terms for a House:
| Requirement | Design Storm |
|---|---|
| Drainage must carry water away without nuisance | **1 in 10 year** (10% AEP) |
| Water must not enter the building | **1 in 50 year** (2% AEP) |

---

### Rainfall Intensities
For sizing gutters and pipes, rainfall intensity values can be sourced from:
- Your **local Territorial Authority (TA)**
- **NIWA's HIRDS** (High Intensity Rainfall Design System)
- Table values in the Acceptable Solution

Where sources differ, use the **most conservative** value.

---

> ⚠️ **This is general Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm against the current MBIE documents and with your designer or drainage engineer, especially for sites near watercourses, in low-lying areas, or with a flooding history — the E1/AS2 Acceptable Solution doesn't cover those situations.

**Source: NZ Building Code Handbook 3rd Ed (Amendment 13), page 49 of 226 & E1 Surface Water (1st edition, amendment 12), pages 56–57 of 59**

## 🏠 Roof/Ceiling Insulation R-Value — New House in Auckland (Climate Zone 1)

This is general Building Code guidance (not project-specific). Here's what the NZ Building Code (Clause H1 – Energy Efficiency) requires:

---

### 📍 Auckland = Climate Zone 1

Auckland falls within **Climate Zone 1** under NZ Building Code Clause H1.

---

### 🔑 Key change — No more "Schedule Method"

As of the **H1/AS1 Sixth Edition**, the old Schedule Method (which used to give simple fixed R-values per zone) has been **removed**. Compliance for housing now uses one of these approaches:

| Method | Document | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Calculation method** | H1/AS1 (6th edition) | Proposed building vs. reference building heat-loss equation |
| **Modelling method** | H1/VM1 (6th edition) | Full energy modelling software |

---

### 📐 Minimum R-values under H1/AS1 (Calculation Method)

Under the calculation method, the **proposed building** roof must meet a hard floor **minimum** of:

> **Roof/ceiling: Construction R-value ≥ R2.6 m²K/W** (all parts, including ceiling perimeter)
> *(Paragraph 2.1.2.11a)*

However, this is a **floor**, not a target. The calculation method works by comparing your whole building against a **reference building** whose roof is set at:

> **Reference building roof: R6.6 m²K/W** *(for Climate Zone 1 — from VM1 Table 2.3.1.2)*

This means in practice, **to pass the overall calculation, a typical Auckland house will need ceiling insulation in the R3.5–R6.6 range** depending on how well the rest of the envelope (walls, floor, glazing) performs. The better your walls and windows, the more flexibility you have on the roof — but R2.6 is the absolute minimum allowed for any part of the roof.

---

### ⚡ Special case: Heated ceilings (e.g. in-ceiling radiant heating)

If you have a **heated ceiling**, the minimum jumps to **R6.6 m²K/W** in Zone 1 (Table 2.1.2.12 of H1/AS1).

---

### 📌 Practical takeaway for your Auckland build

| Roof type | Minimum you can use | Typical target to pass overall calc |
|---|---|---|
| Standard ceiling | **R2.6** (hard floor) | **~R3.5–R6.6** (depending on rest of build) |
| Heated ceiling | **R6.6** | R6.6 |

> 💡 Most designers will target **R3.6 to R6.6** for standard Auckland ceilings to give the overall envelope enough headroom to pass — especially given modern window areas.

---

**Source:** H1 Energy Efficiency AS1 (sixth edition) · pages 3 & 11 of 55; H1 Energy Efficiency VM1 (sixth edition) · page 14 of 37

> ⚠️ **Always confirm with your designer and the current MBIE documents** before specifying materials — H1 has been updated frequently and the specific compliance pathway depends on your building's design. Safety and compliance are ultimately your designer's and consenting authority's call.

## 🚽 Toilets Required for a Household Unit (Dwelling)

Under **Acceptable Solution G1/AS1** (Clause G1 – Personal Hygiene), **Table 1: Number of Sanitary Fixtures**, the requirement for **detached dwellings and multi-unit dwellings** is:

| Building Use | User Group | WC Pans (Unisex) | Basins (Unisex) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detached dwellings & multi-unit dwellings | Occupants | **1** (minimum) | **1** (minimum) |

So the **minimum is 1 toilet (WC pan) and 1 basin** per household unit, regardless of the number of occupants.

---

> ⚠️ **General Building-Code guidance only — not project-specific advice.** Always confirm against the current official MBIE document and with your designer or building consent authority, especially for anything safety-critical.

queriesUsed: maximum open path travel distance escape
answer:
Great question! The answer depends on which **Acceptable Solution** applies to your building (C/AS1 for household units/outbuildings, or C/AS2 for other occupancies), and what **fire protection systems** are installed. Here's a summary:

---

## 🔥 Maximum Open Path Travel Distances

### C/AS1 — Household Units & Outbuildings (Table 3.3.1.1)

| Portion of Escape Route | No System | Type 1 System | Type 1 + Sprinklers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dead End Open Path (DEOP)** | 20 m | 35 m | 40 m |
| **Total Open Path (TOP)** | 50 m | 75 m | 100 m |

---

### C/AS2 — Other Occupancies (Table 3.3.1.1)
Distances vary by **risk group** and **system type**. Key examples:

| Risk Group | No/Type 2 System (DEOP / TOP) | Type 4 or 5 System (DEOP / TOP) | Type 7 System (DEOP / TOP) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SM (e.g. retail/office)** | 25 m / 60 m | 50 m / 120 m | 75 m / 150 m |
| **SL (e.g. large assembly)** | 35 m / 90 m | – | 70 m / 180 m |

> ⚠️ C/AS2 distances also apply **reductions on intermediate floors and stairs/ladders**, so the full table must be consulted for multi-storey buildings.

---

## 📏 How to Measure Open Path Length
- Start measuring from **no more than 1.0 m** from the most remote point in the space
- Measure **around furniture/obstructions** (or orthogonally if locations are unknown)
- The open path **ends** at the start of an exitway, a final exit, or where the route passes into an adjacent firecell

---

> ⚠️ **This is general NZ Building Code guidance, not project-specific advice.** Always confirm against the current official MBIE documents and check with your fire engineer or designer — especially for buildings with multiple risk groups, intermediate floors, or sprinkler systems, as distances can change significantly.
